newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA wants emergency access to brownfields.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA wants emergency access to brownfields.

text.p: The Clinton administration Tuesday raised concern about a bill to redevelop abandoned industrial sites that might limit the federal government's ability to handle dangerous leaks at those sites.

Under a Republican proposal, if a state sets up a voluntary cleanup at a site, then the Environmental Protection Agency would have no authority to respond to a hazardous leak there, EPA acting assistant secretary Timothy Fields said.
Lawmakers proposed the provision to give states the lead in setting cleanup standards in order to encourage rapid redevelopment of the so-called brownfield properties.
They wanted to reassure potential investors that the federal government would not step in after a site had been cleaned and hold them liable for future contamination.
But the EPA wanted to make sure that if there was an emergency, it could enter the site to contain the problem.
"This compromise of public protection is alarming," Fields said in testimony to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
Comparing Republican and Democrat bills, Fields said the administration preferred the Democratic proposal which would provide grants to states and not just to communities.

The administration also wanted to ensure that communities surrounding brownfields would have more of a say in setting cleanup standards and future uses of the properties than the Republican bill would allow.
The Republican and Democrat proposals would both provide up to $200,000 for listing and assessing any brownfields site.

The General Accounting Office, the Congressional watchdog agency, said the $200,000 per property would be sufficient for most sites and was important, because the cost of assessing sites "may be significant enough to discourage developers."
The Clinton administration and lawmakers alike are eager to pass brownfields legislation to help encourage economic development in cities.
